concepts.title: The Age of Revolution and the Birth of Sociology

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Age of Revolution and the Birth of Sociology' refers to.
questions.a: Sociology emerged in the nineteenth century as the child of revolution: the French Revolution upheaval in politics and the industrial transformation of work and city life posed problems no old framework could answer. The first sociologists set out to make sense of this new society -- its division of labour, its rationality, its classes and its despair.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Age of Revolution and the Birth of Sociology'.
questions.a: Sociology was born to explain the modern world at the moment the old order broke apart.

concepts.title: Karl Marx: Classes, Capital and Conflict

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Karl Marx: Classes, Capital and Conflict' refers to.
questions.a: Marx read history as the history of class struggle. Under capitalism the two central classes are the bourgeoisie, owners of the means of production, and the proletariat, sellers of labour power. Surplus value extracted from workers drives accumulation and alienation -- workers estranged from their product, their work and themselves -- until, Marx predicted, the system's contradictions transform it.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Karl Marx: Classes, Capital and Conflict'.
questions.a: Who owns production decides who rules -- class struggle is the motor of history and alienation its human cost.

concepts.title: Emile Durkheim: Social Facts, Solidarity and Suicide

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Emile Durkheim: Social Facts, Solidarity and Suicide' refers to.
questions.a: Durkheim insisted society is a reality of its own: social facts -- norms, institutions, currents of opinion -- exist outside individuals and constrain them, and must be explained by other social facts. He traced the shift from mechanical solidarity (likeness-based, in simple societies) to organic solidarity (interdependence-based, in complex ones) and used suicide rates to show even the most personal act follows social currents.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Emile Durkheim: Social Facts, Solidarity and Suicide'.
questions.a: Society is a thing with its own forces -- even suicide rates follow social facts, not private moods.

concepts.title: Max Weber: Rationalisation, Bureaucracy and the Protestant Ethic

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Max Weber: Rationalisation, Bureaucracy and the Protestant Ethic' refers to.
questions.a: Weber saw modernity as rationalisation -- the relentless organisation of life around efficiency, calculation and rules. Its purest instrument is bureaucracy, hierarchy of offices with written rules and impersonal operation. Against materialism he argued ideas matter too: the Protestant ethic's inner-worldly discipline, he claimed, helped birth the spirit of capitalism.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Max Weber: Rationalisation, Bureaucracy and the Protestant Ethic'.
questions.a: Modernity is the triumph of calculation -- bureaucratic rules everywhere, and even capitalism has a religious biography.
